title: Mutual exclusion, and what it costs
objective: By the end of this lesson you can protect shared data with a mutex, choose the right size of critical section, and give real numbers for what locking costs with and without contention.

blocks.text: A mutex makes a sequence indivisible. While one thread holds it, no other thread can hold it — so the load-add-store from the previous lesson completes with nobody in between. That is the whole idea. The interesting part is where you put it and what it costs.

blocks.caption: The fix for the previous lesson's bug
lines: /* Eight threads now reach exactly 1,600,000, at every optimisation level. */

blocks.text: The rule that keeps this correct

A mutex protects data, not code. Every access to a piece of shared data — reads included — must be made under the same mutex. One thread reading without the lock while another writes with it is still a data race, and thread sanitizer will still report it. Write down which mutex protects which data, in a comment beside the declaration; a lock whose scope lives only in the author's head is how these bugs return.

blocks.title: An uncontended lock never enters the kernel
blocks.text: Seven nanoseconds is far too fast for a system call, and the reason is that Linux mutexes are built on futexes: the fast path is a single atomic operation in user mode, and the kernel is called only when a thread actually has to wait. Verified with strace: 100,000 lock/unlock pairs on one thread produced zero futex system calls, and four threads contending over 400,000 pairs produced only 129. The kernel is involved when there is a genuine wait — not on every lock.

So the cost that matters is contention, not locking. A lock that nobody else wants is nearly free. The way to make a threaded program fast is not to remove locks; it is to reduce how often two threads want the same one at the same moment.

rows: Holding the lock during file or network I/O
Locking and unlocking around each of several related updates
Threads queue behind work that did not need protecting
Another thread sees the data half-updated between them
Symptom: no speedup from adding cores

blocks.caption: Both mistakes, and the fix
lines: /* TOO LARGE: the slow part does not touch shared data */
result = fetch_from_network();      /* 50 ms, holding the lock */
/* Fixed: do the slow work outside */
/* TOO SMALL: two updates that must agree with each other */
/* Between them, the money exists nowhere. Use ONE critical section. */

items: Forgetting to unlock on an early return or error path — every exit from the function must release the lock
Locking the same non-recursive mutex twice in one thread — the thread waits for itself, forever
Two mutexes taken in different orders by different threads — this is deadlock, and it has its own lesson

blocks.title: When an atomic is the better answer
blocks.text: For a single counter or flag, an atomic type is simpler and faster: no lock to forget, no critical section to size. Measured single-threaded: about 2 ns against 7 ns for a mutex pair. But an atomic protects exactly one variable — the moment two values must stay consistent with each other, you need a mutex. Under heavy contention the gap narrows anyway (about 34 ns against 43 ns with eight threads), because both end up fighting over the same cache line.

blocks.title: Fix the race, then measure the lock
steps: Take your racy counter program and add a mutex around the increment
Run at -O0 and -O2 — both should now give exactly 1,600,000, every time
Rebuild with -fsanitize=thread and confirm the warning is gone
Now measure: time 1,000,000 lock/unlock pairs on ONE thread and divide
Repeat with two, four and eight threads and compare per-operation cost
Run: strace -c -f -e trace=futex ./yourprog with one thread, then with four
Confirm the single-threaded run makes no futex calls at all
Finally: move the increment outside the lock but keep the lock — confirm the race returns, proving the lock protects data, not code
blocks.expected: Correct totals at every optimisation level, a silent sanitizer, a per-lock cost that rises sharply with contention and barely at all without it, and a futex count of zero when nothing is contended. The last step is the one that makes the rule stick: the lock did nothing because the data access was not inside it.

cheatsheet: pthread_mutex_lock / unlock around every access to the protected data
A mutex protects DATA, not code — readers must lock too
Document which mutex protects which data, next to the declaration
Measured: ~7 ns per uncontended lock+unlock pair; ~36-43 ns under contention
An uncontended lock makes no system call: 100,000 pairs produced zero futex calls
Contention is the cost, not locking
Too large: never hold a lock across I/O. Too small: keep related updates in one critical section
Release the lock on every exit path, including errors
Atomic for one variable (~2 ns); mutex when two values must stay consistent

checkpoint.prompt: One thread writes a shared counter under a mutex; another reads it without locking. Is that safe?

choices.A: Safe if the value fits in a register
choices.D: No — it is still a data race

checkpoint.explanation: Every access, including reads, must use the same mutex. The mutex protects the data, so it only works if everyone touching that data participates. Thread sanitizer reports exactly this case.

checkpoint.prompt: An uncontended lock/unlock pair costs about 7 ns. Why is that possible when a system call costs far more?

choices.B: The fast path is an atomic operation in user mode

checkpoint.explanation: The kernel is called only when a thread must wait. Verified with strace: 100,000 uncontended lock/unlock pairs produced zero futex system calls. Waiting is what costs; locking by itself is not.

checkpoint.prompt: A service holds a mutex while making a 50 ms network call. What is the symptom?

choices.A: The mutex is released automatically after a timeout
choices.B: Threads serialise behind work that never needed protecting

checkpoint.explanation: Adding cores does not help. Correctness is fine, throughput is not. Do the slow work outside the critical section and take the lock only for the shared update.

checkpoint.prompt: You must subtract from one account and add to another. What is the right locking?

choices.A: Lock and unlock separately around each update
choices.B: No lock if both are atomic
choices.C: One critical section covering both updates
choices.D: An atomic type for each balance

checkpoint.explanation: Between two separate critical sections there is a moment when the money is in neither account, and another thread can observe it. Atomics do not help here: each is individually atomic, and the pair still is not.
